settings.editor:
If your summer electric bills seem to climb faster than the temperature outside, it may be time to take a closer look at your thermostat. 

Every year, homeowners across Springfield, Hendersonville, White House, Gallatin, Portland, and surrounding Middle Tennessee communities start asking the same question:

What's the best thermostat setting for summer?

It's easy to assume that turning the thermostat way down will cool your home faster or that raising it dramatically while you're away will save the most money. In reality, both approaches can create unnecessary strain on your air conditioner and lead to higher energy costs.

A few smart adjustments can help lower cooling costs, improve comfort, and reduce wear on your HVAC system throughout the summer, helping reduce the likelihood of unexpected AC repairs during the hottest months of the year.

At Petitt Heating & Cooling, we help homeowners make these decisions every day. Here's what we typically recommend for staying comfortable without overspending during a Middle Tennessee summer.

settings.title: Quick Answer: What Is the Best Thermostat Setting for Summer?

settings.editor:
For most homeowners, 78°F is the best thermostat setting for summer when you're home. Raise the temperature to 82–85°F when you're away and lower it slightly while sleeping based on personal comfort. 

These settings help reduce energy use while keeping your home comfortable during hot weather.

settings.title: Why Lowering the Thermostat Doesn't Cool Your House Faster

settings.editor:
One of the most common misconceptions homeowners have is that setting the thermostat dramatically lower will cool the house more quickly.

It won't.

Your air conditioner cools at the same rate whether you set the thermostat to 75°F or 65°F. The only difference is how long the system continues running before it shuts off.

That means dropping the temperature far below your target setting often leads to:

  • Higher energy bills
  • Longer run times
  • More wear on your HVAC system
  • Unnecessary strain during extreme heat
If your goal is to reach 74°F, simply set it to 74°F and let the system do its job.

settings.title: The Best Thermostat Setting When You're Home

settings.editor:
For most households, an internal temperature of 78°F offers the best balance between comfort and efficiency.

The U.S. Department of Energy recommends this setting because it allows your air conditioner to operate efficiently while still keeping indoor temperatures comfortable for most people.

That said, comfort matters.

If 78°F feels a little warm for your family, moving the thermostat down a degree or two isn't going to ruin your budget. 

Most homeowners are surprised by how little they notice a one- or two-degree change, especially when it can help reduce cooling costs throughout the summer.

settings.title: The Best Thermostat Setting While You Sleep

settings.editor:
Most people sleep better in a slightly cooler environment.

For many homeowners, the ideal nighttime temperature falls somewhere between 74°F and 78°F

The exact number depends on:

  • Personal preference
  • Bedding
  • Humidity levels
  • Air circulation
This is one area where experimenting can help. A small adjustment can often improve sleep quality without creating a noticeable increase in energy usage.

settings.title: The Best Thermostat Setting When You're Away

settings.editor:
If nobody is home during the day, there's no reason to keep the house at the same temperature.

A common recommendation is 82°F to 85°F while you're away.

This allows your air conditioner to run less frequently while still preventing the home from becoming excessively hot.

Many homeowners make the mistake of turning the thermostat way up before leaving and then cranking it way down when they return.

That's usually not necessary.

Moderate adjustments tend to provide the best balance between comfort and efficiency.

settings.title: What Should You Set Your Thermostat To During Vacation?

settings.editor:
Vacation settings are a little different.

If you'll be gone for several days or longer, most homeowners can safely set the thermostat between 85°F and 88°F

This helps reduce cooling costs while still protecting:

  • Indoor humidity levels
  • Furniture
  • Electronics
  • Flooring
  • Household belongings

You don't want the house to become excessively hot and humid, especially during a Middle Tennessee summer.

The goal is to reduce unnecessary cooling, not completely shut the system down.

settings.title: Why Big Temperature Swings Can Work Against You

settings.editor:
Many homeowners try to save money by making large thermostat adjustments throughout the day.

For example:

  • 68°F at night
  • 85°F during the day
  • 72°F after work

While it sounds efficient, these large swings can actually create comfort problems and force the system to work harder when trying to recover.

Smaller adjustments tend to be more effective.

Instead of constantly chasing different temperatures, focus on maintaining reasonable settings that keep your home comfortable without creating major recovery periods.

settings.title: The Easiest Way to Save Money: Let a Smart Thermostat Do the Work

settings.editor:
This is where smart thermostats really shine.

Instead of manually adjusting temperatures throughout the day, a smart thermostat can automatically follow a schedule based on your routine.

Benefits often include:

  • Automatic temperature adjustments
  • Energy-saving schedules
  • Remote control from your phone
  • Usage tracking
  • Improved comfort consistency

Many homeowners are surprised by how much easier it becomes to manage cooling costs once the thermostat is handling the adjustments automatically.

Perhaps more importantly, it eliminates the guesswork.

No more forgetting to raise the temperature before leaving for work. No more returning from vacation to a house that feels like a sauna.

The system handles it for you.

settings.title: Other Ways to Reduce Summer Cooling Costs

settings.editor:
Thermostat settings matter, but they're only part of the equation.

Your air conditioner also needs proper airflow and efficient operation to keep cooling costs under control.

A few simple habits can help:
A clogged filter restricts airflow and forces your system to work harder than necessary.
Grass clippings, leaves, and debris can reduce efficiency and restrict airflow around the condenser.

settings.title: Close Blinds During Peak Afternoon Heat

settings.editor: Reducing solar heat gain helps your AC maintain indoor temperatures more efficiently.

Small issues often become expensive repairs when they're ignored.

A professional AC tune-up can help identify efficiency problems before they affect comfort or increase utility costs.

settings.title: When Thermostat Adjustments Aren't Solving the Problem

settings.editor:
If your thermostat settings seem reasonable but your energy bills continue climbing, the issue may not be the thermostat at all.

Common problems include:

  • Dirty coils
  • Low refrigerant
  • Duct leaks
  • Poor insulation
  • Aging HVAC equipment
  • Airflow restrictions

If your system struggles to maintain temperature, runs constantly, or creates unusually high energy bills, it's worth having the equipment evaluated.

Sometimes the most effective way to lower cooling costs is solving an underlying HVAC issue.

settings.title: Stay Comfortable This Summer Without Overworking Your AC

settings.editor:
